title: Margaret, are you grieving

segments.voice: Yesterday, my heart in hiding: a priest stirred by a falcon, and a poem dedicated To Christ our Lord. Today, a gentle one. Hopkins meets a child in tears.
screen: `MY HEART IN HIDING.` → `A CHILD IN TEARS.`

segments.voice: Kick through a pile of fall leaves and you hear it: that dry crackle, and a sweet smell of things going brown. To a small child, that sound can be a loss. Hopkins wrote a poem to one, a girl crying in a grove as the leaves come down. It begins: "Margaret, are you grieving / Over Goldengrove unleaving?" He doesn't tell her to cheer up. He asks. And the answer he finds to why she's crying turns the whole poem around. Not the leaves. Her.
screen: `THAT DRY CRACKLE.` → `MARGARET, ARE YOU GRIEVING?` → `NOT THE LEAVES.` → `HER.`

segments.voice: He called the poem Spring and Fall, and gave it a subtitle: to a young child. Some readers hear two falls in that title: the season of dropping leaves, and the Fall in Genesis, the story where death enters human life. He tells Margaret that as the heart grows older it will come to such sights colder. Grown-ups stop crying over leaves. And yet, he says, you will weep and know why. Then the turn: "Sorrow's springs are the same." Whatever we grieve, it rises from one source. And the last lines: "It is the blight man was born for, / It is Margaret you mourn for." Before she has the words, the leaves are teaching her that she will fall too. That's the Christian teaching under the poem, the doctrine of the Fall. After the first disobedience, still in the garden, God says to the man in Genesis: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Catholics and some other Christians hear words like these on Ash Wednesday, as ash is pressed on the forehead. The teaching doesn't pretend death away. It names it plainly, and then it hopes past it. Notice how Hopkins does it. He doesn't fix her sorrow or explain it away, and he doesn't rush her to heaven. He calls her by name, and he stays with her in it.
screen: `SPRING AND FALL: TO A YOUNG CHILD.` · `SORROW'S SPRINGS ARE THE SAME.` · `DUST THOU ART.` · `HE CALLS HER BY NAME.` · then, large: `IT IS MARGARET YOU MOURN FOR.`

segments.voice: Find one thing that was once growing: a leaf, a petal, a dried herb, the stem of old flowers. For two minutes, hold it, feel how light it is, and listen to it crackle between your fingers. If someone you love is sad right now, a child or a grown-up, hold them in mind too, without trying to fix it.
Margaret: the child in Hopkins's poem, weeping over the leaves of Goldengrove. The poem never tells us more about her. Some readers hear in her any child meeting the fall.
For the road: it is Margaret you mourn for, and the poet doesn't hurry her. Until tomorrow.
